notes:
Maintainer risk: MEDIUM — three P0 findings cluster around two systemic issues (RFC-conformance lints that silently assume use-case context; cert hashing that silently produces a sentinel on encode failure). Both have well-bounded fixes. Six P1 findings are operator-facing UX issues with the deviation/scope/runner machinery — visible to operators when configurations don't fire as expected. Pre-1.0 framing applies: most of these are best fixed now while breaking changes are still free.
Confidence: 80% chance of missed bug. Least confident flags: PKIX-hy2e.12 (mailbox_equivalent A-label/U-label edge case — I haven't run the real-world cert corpus through it). The OSCAL Profile composition logic in oscal/profile.rs is non-trivial (recursive imports, cycle detection, merge ordering across layered profiles) and I did not exhaustively trace every combination — the round-trip tests cover the happy paths but I did not verify that 'inner override + outer override on same param' applies in the documented order under all import topologies. Uncertainty driven by: not running the test suite under proptest or fuzz; not having dumped a real CT-log corpus through the lints to surface real-world false positives. Would raise confidence if: (a) fuzz the OSCAL parsers (parse.rs + profile.rs) with cargo-fuzz against malformed JSON; (b) run pkix-difftest with these lints enabled against the PKITS and x509-limbo corpora to spot false positives I missed in code reading; (c) verify the apply_parameter_overrides atomicity claim empirically by writing the cross-profile multi-set-parameter test the doc says is needed.
API contract risk: MEDIUM — the engine is correctness-sound but several public structs lack #[non_exhaustive] (PKIX-hy2e.22, .31) and one trait method (Lint::id) is over-restricted on lifetime (.24). These are pre-1.0-free fixes that get harder after 1.0. The check_shape Ok/Err discard pattern (.25) and the Deviation construct-vs-validate split (.27) are caller-facing footguns that produce defensive-code-forcing shapes. None block 1.0 architecturally; all are tractable fixes that should be addressed before stability commitment.
API contract confidence: 75% chance of missed issue. Least confident flags: (a) PKIX-hy2e.30 (DeviationScope.kind allocation — substantive forward-compat argument but the immediate engineering cost is small enough that operators might reasonably defer); (b) PKIX-hy2e.32 (serde_json::Value coupling — the engineering reality is unavoidable and the fix is documentation, so labeling this 'API contract risk' is somewhat soft). Uncertainty driven by: (a) I did not enumerate every public method on every public struct — sampled the high-leverage ones (Lint trait, LintRunner, Finding, Deviation, OSCAL entry points); (b) did not exhaustively trace which fields in which structs are populated by external code paths (e.g., does any code outside the crate construct Finding directly? rustdoc examples and tests do, but real callers might not); (c) did not check the dev-dep / doc-test compile fixtures to verify that the documented examples actually exercise the construction patterns I'm critiquing. Would raise confidence if: (i) ran cargo +nightly rustdoc to confirm no public items lack docs that I missed; (ii) ran cargo public-api against a pinned 0.8.0 to enumerate exactly which symbols are public; (iii) checked downstream consumers (pkix-chain, pkix-lint-cabf) for actual construction-site dependency on the affected types.
Idiom rating: ACCEPTABLE — pkix-lint is mostly idiomatic Rust. The five idiom findings filed (.34 .35 .36 .37 .38) cluster around two real concerns: (a) error info discarded at the parse/match boundary (DER errors, mailbox parse errors), and (b) modest DRY/style cleanup (hex duplication, FQ Cow paths). No unsafe, no panics outside test/unreachable arms, no Box<dyn Error>-in-library, no broken iterator/collection idioms, no macro abuse. The crate forbids unsafe at the crate root (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]) and the trait surface uses Send+Sync, object-safety, and provided defaults correctly. The five flagged items are all worth fixing pre-1.0 while breaking changes remain free.
Rust idiom confidence: 85% chance of missed issue. Least confident flags: PKIX-hy2e.37 (mailbox_equivalent stringly-typed error) — this is the kind of internal-helper choice that genuinely admits multiple defensible answers; flagged because the workspace's larger pattern (deviation.rs ParseError, ParameterError) prefers typed errors, but reasonable maintainers could leave the &'static str helper alone. PKIX-hy2e.38 (FQ Cow path) — this is clippy-tier cosmetic; the engineering basis is 'less reading friction across 20 sites in lib.rs', which is real but minor. Uncertainty driven by: (a) did not run cargo clippy --all-features -- -W clippy::pedantic on the diff; clippy may catch additional small wins (let-else-could-be-let, unnecessary-cast, redundant-clone-in-tests, etc.) that a focused machine pass would find; (b) did not enumerate every #[allow] attribute in the crate to verify each is justified; (c) did not check the deviation.rs/parse.rs/profile.rs hex helpers against the rfc-conformance pass for behavioural divergence (e.g., one might tolerate whitespace where another doesn't). Would raise confidence if: running cargo +nightly clippy --all-features --all-targets -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery and reviewing the output of any -W clippy::* lints currently allowed at the crate level. The crate already enforces #![warn(missing_docs, rust_2018_idioms)] but does not enforce clippy::pedantic.
Crypto-security supplement complete. Filed 4 issues (.39 .40 .41 .42), all under label crypto-security.

Scope reality: pkix-lint is a lint engine over already-parsed x509-cert::Certificate structures. It has no key material, no RNG, no persistent secret storage, no logging of secrets. The crypto-security surface is narrow: SHA-256 over cert DER, SHA-256-derived UUIDv8 for evidence packs, OSCAL JSON parsing as the untrusted-input boundary, and post-parse re-decoding of extension payload bytes.

Sections covered:
- A (key material lifecycle): N/A — no secrets in this crate.
- B (side-channel hygiene): N/A — no secret-dependent branches; cert content is public.
- C (untrusted input at protocol boundaries): two findings filed.
  - .39 P2: resolve_profile_inner has no recursion depth limit; deeply chained distinct Profile imports stack-overflow even though cycles are caught.
  - .40 P3: hex_decode pre-allocates Vec::with_capacity(s.len()/2) without an explicit upper bound on the caller-controlled hex string length. Defense-in-depth; serde_json's own parse already bounds the realistic vector.
- D (random source quality): N/A — no RNG.
- E (persistent storage of secrets): N/A — no secrets stored.
- F (logging output safety): N/A — Finding::Display interpolates lint_id and message; certificate-derived strings are public.
- G (algorithm and parameter choice): two findings filed.
  - .41 P3: UUIDv8 seed concatenation has delimiter-ambiguous field boundaries; defense-in-depth against future field additions making collision tractable.
  - .42 P3: UUIDv8 seeds use usize::to_le_bytes — UUIDs differ across 32-bit and 64-bit hosts, breaking documented provenance determinism.

Time spent: ~25 minutes — read main source modules end-to-end plus targeted greps for unwrap, from_der, recursion, allocation. Section C took the most time (read oscal/parse.rs and oscal/profile.rs end-to-end including all parse_* helpers). Sections A/B/D/E/F were ruled out by inspection in under 5 minutes each because the crate's data model excludes the relevant code paths.

Read all relevant code paths vs only the diff: I read all the touched files in this scope range end-to-end (lib.rs, deviation.rs, oscal/parse.rs, oscal/profile.rs, oscal/emit.rs, rfc5280.rs/rfc6125.rs/rfc8398.rs untrusted-input shapes). The crypto-security supplement specifically calls out that defects often live in unchanged code that the diff touches through helpers; the cert_sha256_of helper already-flagged at .2 is the canonical example.

Probability of missed P0: ~5%. Justification: no key material or secret in scope; the high-leverage Section A and B classes don't apply; Section C surface is small (OSCAL JSON, post-parse extension re-decode, deviation scope matching) and was read exhaustively. Most plausible miss vector is a panic-able path I missed in extension parsing, but the rfc5280/rfc6125/rfc8398 lints uniformly use .ok_or, .as_ref(), .find, and match on Result rather than .unwrap() — checked via grep, 0 production-side unwraps outside cert_sha256_of (already flagged at .2). The Severity::Fatal pathway exists for parser-failure escalation if the runner ever needs to propagate one.

If X > 20% rule: 5% is well under 20%. No P1 needed to schedule deeper pass or external review.

Sections worth deeper attention if budget allowed: Section C — the OSCAL Catalog parser (lint_ids_from_catalog) and Profile parser were read but not fuzzed. A 10-minute cargo-fuzz run against parse_risk and resolve_profile would raise confidence to ~99%. Filing a probe-bd-issue for fuzzing is reasonable but I am leaving that decision to the primary epic owner since fuzzing is outside the read-only scope of this supplement and the existing epic's calibration already notes that fuzz coverage is a known gap.
